messages.subject: Can stan be used for a fast replacement of linear/nonlinear regression?
parts:
Hi,

I've been using lm (linear modeling) and nnls (nonnegative least squares) in R, and was looking for a faster alternative, and found stan. The first impression I got is that stan was not primarily designed to do the job that ln and nnls do, am I (hopefully) wrong about this?

As an alternative to R's nnls, I tried the following stan model:

data {
  int<lower=0> N; // number of data items
  int<lower=0> K; // number of predictors
  matrix[N,K] x; // predictor matrix
  vector[N] y; // outcome vector
}
parameters {
  vector<lower=0>[K] beta; // coefficients for predictors
  real<lower=0> sigma; // error scale
}
model {
  y ~ normal(x * beta, sigma); // likelihood
}

Using the above code in rstan, I used optimizing() function to perform the job of nnls. For N=250 and K=400, it takes 0.02 s for nnls, while the above stan equivalent takes over 3.5 s.

Am I doing this wrong, or is stan not designed to solve this problem?

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Why is Stan's optimizer so slow?
parts:
Hi, I don’t know how nnls works, but Stan _should_ be able to fast optimization.  Stan can do logistic regression faster than R’s glm function but maybe that’s not the best comparison because R’s glm function is notoriously clunky and slow.  I suppose that nnls is faster.

But I don’t think we should be taking hundreds of times longer than R’s optimizer.  So this does seem to be something we should look into!
A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can stan be used for a fast replacement of linear/nonlinear regression?
parts:
Hi David,

The quick answer is that Stan isn't designed to solve any one specific model, it's designed to be able to work with a very general class of models.  For specific models, like this one, packages which focus on solving such models are very likely to work faster.  The power of Stan comes when you want to start making changes to this model to better suite your data, e.g., a student_t model, non-linear transforms of the parameters, hierarchical models, etc.

This particular model may be hard for Stan because of the way constraints are handled using a log transform.  This makes it effectively impossible for beta to ever be zero.  If the data strongly supports that, the optimizer could end up spending a long time trying to get close to zero.

Now, that said, we would like to make Stan as competitive as possible even with these simple models for which there may be specialized approaches.  So, can you send along any scripts, data, initialization, etc that you were using for this so that we can look into it?  Also any printed output from your Stan run would be helpful.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can stan be used for a fast replacement of linear/nonlinear regression?
parts:
Andrew,

NNLS is definitely using a specialized algorithm for non-negatively constrained linear least squares.  See http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-negative_least_squares#Algorithms 

There are definitely things we can do about it.  Simple linear bound constraints (i.e., lb <= x <= ub) are actually pretty easy to handle in optimization algorithms.  The issue is the plumbing necessary to take a model and represent the constraints that way instead of how we're currently doing it with non-linear transforms.  That might be worth doing as it would also allow us to play with other ways of sampling in the presence of such constraints.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can stan be used for a fast replacement of linear/nonlinear regression?
parts:
Yup.  For HMC-stan it makes sense to work on the unconstrained scale.  (We’ve also talked on occasion about implementing bouncing for constrained parameters, but maybe that makes the algorithm too messy.)  But for point estimation, boundary estimates come up a lot.  Sometimes we go to some trouble to avoid boundary estimates (as with our boundary-avoiding priors for group-level variance parameters), other times boundary estimates are considered a plus (for example, lasso).  So, indeed, maybe we should think about implementing constrained optimization in Stan.  Perhaps, for example, the Stan program could be altered by including a tag for each parameter that we want to enforce will _not_ be transformed.
A

All the information is already in the model in the form of constraints on variables, so tagging isn't really required.  The key is making the information explicitly available to the optimizer or sampler (if desired) instead of always automatically transforming things into an unconstrained space.  This is basically the same plumbing that would be needed if someone wanted to implement bouncing for constrained parameters.

I guess tags could be useful if someone wanted to explicitly request something be transformed to an unconstrained scale for some reason or if they explicitly wanted boundary values included/excluded.

parts: Hi David.  We just discussed this problem in the Stan meeting and Bob came up with a clever solution which would allow Stan to optimize on the original scale.  The trick is simply to not specify the bound on beta but instead to put the constraint into the model.  Something like this:

data {
  int<lower=0> N; // number of data items
  int<lower=0> K; // number of predictors
  matrix[N,K] x; // predictor matrix
  vector[N] y; // outcome vector

real<lower=0> A; //set A to be really large to make a hard constraint of beta to be positive
}
parameters {
  vector[K] beta; // coefficients for predictors

real<lower=0> sigma; // error scale
}
model {

for (k in 1:K)
    increment_log_prob(log_inv_logit(A*b[k]))

y ~ normal(x * beta, sigma); // likelihood
}

Ummm, maybe I’m bumbling the details here, but the idea is that you run it and specify some large positive value of A, which has the effect of enforcing positivity on the estimate of the coefficients b[k].

This is a hack (presumably it would make more sense for Stan to automatically increase A while it’s running) but it might be worth a try.  If the problem with the original run was that Stan was taking forever to get to the boundary, this could help things.
A

Hi Guys,

Thanks a lot for the interesting discussion, and sorry for the delay. I have prepared a minimal example you can download here, which compares nnls with a nonnegative constrained stan optimization problem.

I tried to make the stan problem as simple as possible, and went with maximum likelihood estimation (squared_error <- dot_self(y - x * beta)) with a simple nonnegative constraint on beta (<lower=0>).

Here are the main problems:
  • Stan is a few orders slower than nnls.
  • Stan solutions do not seem correct:  fitted values look nothing like y, while nnls fitted values seem to be a right solution.
  • Stan is inconsistent: fitted values vary wildly an widely with every run. The answers are very different each time, and so are the processing times.
The above problems almost disappear when the stan problem is unconstrained.

Andrew: I have tried your suggestion, unfortunately it did not work. What you suggested is basically a heavily penalized unconstrained regularized linear regression. This is intrusive to the fitted values, and changes their shape (even with dot_self() version).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can stan be used for a fast replacement of linear/nonlinear regression?
parts:
Hi David,

So I took a look at what was going on with this case and I've found a few things

- The optimal solution (from nnls) is very sparse, i.e., all but maybe a dozen coefficients are zero.  This solution is going to be very hard (if not impossible) for Stan to reach using the parameterization (using lower=0) that you used in the basic model.  This is because in the unconstrained domain, a parameter needs to effectively get to infinity for it to be zero.  Worse though is that it is definitely possible for it to converge to bad solution due to numerical issues.  This happens when the unconstrained parameter x becomes sufficiently negative that exp(x) underflows and is numerically zero.  The problem is that then the derivative wrt x becomes zero and this parameter will *never* change again.  So, if the optimizer over shoots for a parameter, it can get stuck in a bad place.  Worse, this can't be easily diagnosed because it's gradient will appear to be zero!

To summarize for users:  If you are optimizing and expect your solution to end up on a constraint boundary, *do not* use Stan's "lower=" or "upper=" constraints.  They will almost certainly result in failures and it's likely that it there will be no obvious indication that it's failed.

For stan-dev:  It would be really nice if we could handle simple bound constraints directly in the optimizer.  One more thing to put on the (ever-growing) todo list...  Also, it may be worth checking for underflow in exp() and throwing an exception.  I hate to do it because it's going to potentially really hurt performance, but issues like this seem to pop up more than I'd like.

- Using a squared or fabs parameterization avoids this issue for the most part.  You can't use init=0 in this case because the gradients are all zero there, but otherwise it will work better.  However for it to have a chance of working, you need to normalize your data a bit.  Right now the scale on the data is huge which is blowing out the gradients and making it difficult for the optimizer to make initial progress.  You should normalize your data to have a std dev of 1.  Note that this can even be done in the transformed data block of the Stan model to make it easier.

- This model is sufficiently large that you'll want to use LBFGS instead of BFGS.  On my machine LBFGS is about 40 times faster for your data.  As an added bonus, because LBFGS is often better at adapting to curvature changes, it actually gets to a better optimum for me.

- Also, be aware of the convergence criteria.  They are set to values which are reasonable but certainly may need to be adjusted for different problems.  If the optimizer is stopping but not at the right solution, consider adjusting (or turning off) some of the convergence tests.  E.G., for your data and model I found turning off the relative convergence tests to be useful.  See also normalizing your data.

- The model could be made a bit faster by using squared_distance() instead of dot_self().  (Not a huge speedup, but it will help a little bit.)

Play around a bit with normalizing your data, using the squared() parameterization and LBFGS and let us know how it goes.

Cheers,
Marcus

Hi David,

So I took a look at what was going on with this case and I've found a few things

- The optimal solution (from nnls) is very sparse, i.e., all but maybe a dozen coefficients are zero.  This solution is going to be very hard (if not impossible) for Stan to reach using the parameterization (using lower=0) that you used in the basic model.  This is because in the unconstrained domain, a parameter needs to effectively get to infinity for it to be zero.  Worse though is that it is definitely possible for it to converge to bad solution due to numerical issues.  This happens when the unconstrained parameter x becomes sufficiently negative that exp(x) underflows and is numerically zero.  The problem is that then the derivative wrt x becomes zero and this parameter will *never* change again.  So, if the optimizer over shoots for a parameter, it can get stuck in a bad place.  Worse, this can't be easily diagnosed because it's gradient will appear to be zero!

To summarize for users:  If you are optimizing and expect your solution to end up on a constraint boundary, *do not* use Stan's "lower=" or "upper=" constraints.  They will almost certainly result in failures and it's likely that it there will be no obvious indication that it's failed.

For stan-dev:  It would be really nice if we could handle simple bound constraints directly in the optimizer.  One more thing to put on the (ever-growing) todo list...  Also, it may be worth checking for underflow in exp() and throwing an exception.  I hate to do it because it's going to potentially really hurt performance, but issues like this seem to pop up more than I'd like.

- Using a squared or fabs parameterization avoids this issue for the most part.  You can't use init=0 in this case because the gradients are all zero there, but otherwise it will work better.  However for it to have a chance of working, you need to normalize your data a bit.  Right now the scale on the data is huge which is blowing out the gradients and making it difficult for the optimizer to make initial progress.  You should normalize your data to have a std dev of 1.  Note that this can even be done in the transformed data block of the Stan model to make it easier.

- This model is sufficiently large that you'll want to use LBFGS instead of BFGS.  On my machine LBFGS is about 40 times faster for your data.  As an added bonus, because LBFGS is often better at adapting to curvature changes, it actually gets to a better optimum for me.

- Also, be aware of the convergence criteria.  They are set to values which are reasonable but certainly may need to be adjusted for different problems.  If the optimizer is stopping but not at the right solution, consider adjusting (or turning off) some of the convergence tests.  E.G., for your data and model I found turning off the relative convergence tests to be useful.  See also normalizing your data.

- The model could be made a bit faster by using squared_distance() instead of dot_self().  (Not a huge speedup, but it will help a little bit.)

Play around a bit with normalizing your data, using the squared() parameterization and LBFGS and let us know how it goes.

Cheers,
Marcus

Sure. The question is general and the following models are not meant to be data-specific. The only criteria I used here is implicit nonnegative parameters through sqrt_beta, as the outcome of this discussion thread.

(1) y_1 = x * beta_1, y_2 = x * beta_2, ..., y_L = x * beta_L

data {
  int<lower=0> N; // number of data items
  int<lower=0> K; // number of predictors
  int<lower=1> L; // number of outcome collections
  matrix[N,K] x; // predictor matrix
  vector[K] y[L]; // outcome vectors
}
parameters {
  vector[K] sqrt_beta[L];
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[K] beta[L];
  for(l in 1:L)
    for(k in 1:K)
      beta[l][k] <- square(sqrt_beta[l][k]);
}
model {
  for(l in 1:L)
    increment_log_prob(-squared_distance(y[l], x) * beta[L]));
}

In the above model, we have a shared x matrix. For L ~ 1e3, what can we do to avoid re-computations?


(2) y = x_1 * beta_1, y = x_2 * beta_2, ..., y = x_L * beta_L

data {
  int<lower=0> N; // number of data items
  int<lower=0> K; // number of predictors
  int<lower=1> L; // number of predictors collections
  matrix[N,K] x[L]; // predictor matrix
  vector[K] y; // outcome vector
}
parameters {
  vector[K] sqrt_beta[L];
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[K] beta[L];
  for(l in 1:L)
    for(k in 1:K)
      beta[l][k] <- square(sqrt_beta[l][k]);
}
model {
  for(l in 1:L)

In the above model, we have shared y. I believe model (1) would be more efficient if we could take advantage of caching some shared-variable-related computations.
